items.title: iPhone 18 Pro @ $1,199 packs in more AI
items.summary: Apple has introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, bringing major upgrades across performance, on-device AI, cameras, battery life and thermal management. At the heart of the new Pro models is the A20 Pro chip, which delivers significant gains in CPU, GPU and neural processing while enabling more powerful on-device Apple Intelligence features. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 in the US.The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max also introduce a new 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture, giving users greater control over light, depth of field and the overall look of photos and videos. Apple has also added new professional camera controls, improved video capabilities and enhanced AI-powered photography tools.iPhone 18 Pro launched at $ 1,119 The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are powered by the new A20 Pro chip, built around a redesigned architecture focused on performance and efficiency. The chip features a six-core CPU with new performance and efficiency cores, with CPU performance up to 20% faster than the previous generation. The GPU has also received a major upgrade, with a seven-core design delivering significant gains in graphics performance and AI-powered image generation.The new neural engine is specifically designed for on-device AI workloads, with a 32-core design and support for advanced 8-bit floating-point operations. Together, the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine improvements make the A20 Pro significantly more capable of running demanding Apple Intelligence features directly on the iPhone. Apple has also increased memory bandwidth by 50%, helping the device handle larger AI models and demanding applications more efficiently.More powerful Apple Intelligence and SiriThe new Pro models bring deeper Apple Intelligence capabilities, including access to Apple's latest Foundation models and more powerful on-device AI models. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro can run its most advanced on-device models yet, enabling features such as enhanced image generation, smarter photo editing and more capable Siri interactions.Siri is also getting a major upgrade. Users can interact with Siri more naturally, continue conversations across Apple devices and use the assistant to take actions across supported apps. Siri can understand information displayed through the camera and help users act on what they see. Apple Intelligence also brings more personalised capabilities, including creating automations through natural-language instructions, finding information across apps and generating images through Image Playground.Apple says the new capabilities will work across more than 3,000 apps, allowing developers to integrate Apple's AI features into everyday workflows.New 48MP camera with variable apertureOne of the biggest upgrades comes to the camera system. The iPhone 18 Pro introduces a new 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture, giving users more control over how much light enters the camera and how much of the scene remains in focus.The variable-aperture system can automatically adjust depending on the scene, while also allowing users to manually control the aperture for greater creative flexibility. A wider aperture can create a shallower depth of field, while a narrower aperture can keep more of the scene in focus. Apple has also introduced new Pro controls, allowing users to manually adjust settings such as white balance, exposure, histogram and shutter speed.For video creators, the iPhone 18 Pro adds more advanced controls and improved cinematic capabilities. Users can adjust shutter speed for motion blur, while AI-powered smart focus tracking can maintain focus on moving subjects. The new system also supports improved Dolby Vision HDR video and enhanced audio recording capabilities.New tools for photographersApple is also expanding its computational photography capabilities. Photographic Styles now offer additional control over texture and grain, allowing users to create more distinctive looks while retaining control over colour and skin tones. The iPhone 18 Pro also introduces a new approach to preserving image authenticity. Apple says captured images can retain additional information that can be used to verify what was actually recorded by the camera.Together with the new variable-aperture camera and Pro controls, Apple says the system is designed to offer greater flexibility for both everyday photography and professional workflows.Improved thermal managementApple has redesigned the thermal architecture of the iPhone 18 Pro to help sustain the higher performance of the A20 Pro chip. The new thermal system features a next-generation vapour chamber with three times the surface area of the system used in the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple has also introduced new thermal materials, including a nano-twin copper material designed to move heat away from the display more effectively. The company says the redesigned thermal system can deliver up to a 40% improvement in sustained performance compared with the previous-generation Pro model.Longest battery life ever on an iPhoneBattery life is another major focus of the new Pro models. The iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max delivers up to 45 hours, giving the Max model the longest battery life ever offered on an iPhone. Apple has also improved charging, with the iPhone 18 Pro capable of reaching 50% charge in around 15 minutes under supported conditions.More connectivity and iOS 27 featuresThe iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also benefit from new software and connectivity features in iOS 27. Apple says AirDrop transfers are up to 80% faster, while connectivity has been improved with smarter transitions between Wi-Fi networks. A new feature called iPhone Handoff allows a single phone number to be used across two iPhones, with the number becoming active on whichever iPhone the user picks up. The Pro models also feature an upgraded Dynamic Island, while iOS 27 brings further customisation and improvements across apps including Mail and other system experiences.iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max price and availabilityThe iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 in the US. Pre-orders for both models begin September 12, with availability starting September 18. With the A20 Pro chip, deeper on-device Apple Intelligence, a new variable-aperture 48MP camera, improved thermal architecture and the longest battery life ever on an iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max represent Apple's biggest Pro upgrade across performance, photography and AI.

items.title: Microsoft is funding a bet on mud
items.summary: Warblers and sparrows call across the treetops at sunrise. Deer browse the shrubs. Black bears turn over roots for insects. Above ground, this stretch of North Carolina's Inner Banks looks like farmland, cotton and soybeans and corn running to the horizon.The reason scientists and investors have converged on this 60-square-kilometre tract is underneath it: dense, spongy peat, up to five metres deep, the Associated Press reported.Decades ago, an abandoned farming venture cut 80 kilometres of ditches through the site and drained the water out of soil that had taken thousands of years to accumulate. That left it exposed to drought and fire, altered the habitat, and turned a carbon store into a carbon source. The site now emits about 130,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year."Our goal is for perpetuity to conserve these lands so they can't become oil and gas fields, so they're not mined for phosphorus or turned into parking lots and shopping centers," Tripp Wall, chief executive of the Colorado-based company Pantheon Regeneration, told AP. He described peatlands as underappreciated systems that had been climatologically resilient for 10,000 to 15,000 years "until we screwed them up."Why peat matters more than forestPeatlands cover roughly 3% of the planet's land surface. They hold close to a third of all soil carbon, which is about twice as much as the biomass of every forest on Earth combined, according to the UN Environment Programme.The mechanism is simple. When peat is waterlogged, decomposing plant matter sits in an oxygen-starved environment and the gases stay trapped, while the vegetation on the surface keeps pulling carbon dioxide out of the air. Drain it and the process reverses.That reversal is now a significant emissions source in its own right. UNEP's Global Peatlands Assessment put emissions from drained and degraded peatlands at around 4% of annual human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, from an area equal to roughly 0.4% of the world's land surface. The AP report cites a higher current figure of about 6% of the annual global total.Two-thirds of temperate peatlands, mostly in Europe and the United States, have been dewatered. About 45% of tropical peatlands have been similarly disturbed. Boreal peatlands in Canada and Russia remain roughly 90% intact but face thawing permafrost, intensifying fires and pressure from mining and critical minerals exploration.Only 17% of the world's peatlands sit inside a protected area, according to a study published in Conservation Letters, the journal of the Society for Conservation Biology, in February 2025. For comparison, protected areas cover 38% of tropical forests, 42% of mangroves and 50% of saltmarshes."This is the black gold"Neal Flanagan pushes a metal tube down through roots and buried logs until it sinks about a metre, then pulls out a core packed with black soil. Near the top it is dry, full of dead fibres from wood fern and blueberry. The middle is crumbly and odourless, flecked with charcoal from old fires. The saturated bottom is half carbon and has the consistency of axle grease."This is the black gold," said Duke University ecologist Curtis Richardson, letting ancient peat ooze from his fist. Its "magnitude and importance cannot be underestimated," he told AP.The North Carolina variety, called Pocosin peat, formed from coastal pine forests and evergreen shrubs decaying over millennia. Domed peatlands of this type exist only along the Eastern Seaboard. In North Carolina alone, 17,700 kilometres of canals drain peatlands into coastal estuaries, Richardson said.Fires that burn underground for monthsSaturated peat is close to fireproof. Only surface vegetation and a few inches of peat burn, releasing nutrients and regenerating seed banks.Dry peat is a different proposition. Fire moves underground and can smoulder for weeks or months, drying out and consuming even the saturated layers below.A 2008 fire that started during a drought burned above ground for three months and smouldered underground for four more, damaging over a quarter of the neighbouring Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge and dropping the ground level by several feet in places, refuge manager Sarah Toner said. Where water-level restoration had already begun, the fire burned less deeply.A more recent fire burned about 800 hectares nearby four years ago, lowering the ground by half a metre in places. The North Carolina Forest Service and other agencies put it out in roughly three weeks by pumping water from nearby lakes."We'll lose 5, 6 feet of peat in a matter of weeks, which equates to millions of tons of carbon loss, ancient carbon loss that we simply can't ever get back in human lifetimes," Richardson said.That risk is why Pantheon is prioritising drained sites over intact ones. "There's this urgency to start with what's degraded now," Wall said, "before it goes away."The business modelThe restoration itself is not novel. Pantheon plans to block the ditches to raise the water table, then remove invasive species and replant native grasses and flowers, an approach modelled on projects run by nonprofits and government agencies, including at the adjacent 453-square-kilometre Pocosin Lakes refuge, one of the largest peatland restorations in the United States. That refuge supports red wolves, yellow pitcher plants and Atlantic white cedar, and has become a stopover for migrating tundra swans.What is different is how Pantheon intends to pay for it. The company plans to sell carbon credits to technology companies and other corporations offsetting their own emissions, then use the proceeds to restore and permanently conserve about 4,047 square kilometres of peatland from Virginia to northern Florida over the next decade. Microsoft is among the investors providing initial capital for land acquisition, Wall said. Each credit represents one tonne.Carbon credits carry a reputational problem. Over the years, some programmes have been found to overstate how much carbon they captured, and others were outright fraudulent.Pantheon says its credits will be scientifically verified, drawing on Richardson's decades of data on carbon loss at the site, continuous groundwater monitoring, a tower measuring gas absorbed and released, computer modelling and core sampling, with results checked by an outside third party.What comes backSteve Apfelbaum, a plant and animal ecologist running breeding and migratory bird surveys at the site, stops his SUV on a rutted lane to listen. He picks out prairie warblers, a species in decline."We heard hundreds of them today," he said. "What that tells me is that this ecosystem is really important" for their migration. He also hears Nashville warblers, which call from treetops but nest in cavities in the peat.Native reptiles, plants, fish and insects should follow, said Vladimir Roosevelt, Pantheon's operations director. The company released a pair of red wolves two years ago that have since had pups.All of it, Apfelbaum said, depends on getting the water back into the ground first, a solution he argued gets less attention than tree planting."We've all been bear-hugged and distracted by trees," he said, "when it's really soil and peat that hold the most carbon."(With inputs from AP)

Americares lands its biggest gift ever
items.summary: A Connecticut family that will not be identified has given $50 million to the American aid group Americares, the largest single donation in the organisation's 47-year history, the Associated Press reported on Wednesday.The gift lands at an unusual moment. Most global health organisations have spent the past year and a half contracting. Americares is now planning to expand."They definitely understood the moment and wanted to do more to respond to that," Christine Squires, the president and chief executive of Americares, told AP of the donor. The family has been associated with the organisation for three decades and is, in her words, very savvy about global health.Also read: MacKenzie Scott's $100 million donation helped wipe out $40 billion in medical debt—here’s how Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife's strategy worksHalf the money will go toward the group's target of helping 100 million people access quality healthcare by 2030, largely by supplying medicines and equipment to its network of more than 4,000 health centres. The focus will be on under-funded countries in sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, North Africa, Asia and Latin America. Americares also plans to increase support for health centres inside the United States, in states where it expects a rise in the number of residents without insurance. The other half goes into the endowment.What was lostAmericares drew roughly 10% of its funding from the US government before the cuts, Squires told AP. The shortfall showed up as cancelled work.A maternal care project in Tanzania lost its support last year. Medical clinics in Colombia serving Venezuelan migrants stayed open for several months on private money before closing. A planned five-year collaboration to build a more resilient medical supply chain across Gaza was scrapped entirely.The organisation now funds itself entirely through individual donors, corporations and private foundations, which Squires said matters as it responds to more than 20 active emergencies, among them the Nepal floods and the Ebola outbreak in Congo.Founded in 1979 and headquartered in Stamford, Connecticut, Americares says it has delivered more than $17 billion in humanitarian aid across 164 countries.The bigger holeThe gift is the latest in a series of private interventions since the Trump administration dismantled the US Agency for International Development in early 2025. The scale of what was withdrawn makes the arithmetic difficult. US foreign aid totalled about $64 billion in 2023, the most recent year with comprehensive figures.Private money has moved, though unevenly. British hedge fund manager Chris Hohn stepped in to keep production running at MANA Nutrition, one of two American manufacturers of the therapeutic peanut paste used to treat severe child malnutrition, after US stop-work orders halted their lines. Hohn had already given the organisation more than $250 million before the crisis.A group of former USAID staff, working outside office hours or after being fired, assembled a list of 80 high-impact programmes and took it to private donors. Their effort, Project Resource Optimization, mobilised more than $110 million in grants, with other emergency funds raising at least $15 million more, taking the total past $125 million within eight months.In March 2025, Jacklyn and Miguel Bezos, the parents of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, committed up to $500 million to UNICEF's Child Nutrition Fund, structured as a one-to-one match designed to draw in other donors. It was, by UNICEF's own account, the largest investment the agency had ever received from a family. The Gates Foundation, separately, narrowed its priorities.Susan Appe, an associate professor of public administration and policy at the University at Albany who researches how nonprofits handle shifting donor-country priorities, told AP that global health has drawn most of the large donors' attention, which she called reasonable given that lives are at stake. But she said the philanthropic response overall has been slower than researchers in her field expected."I think that a lot of philanthropy scholars like myself have been a bit disappointed with the lag of response," she told AP. "It's kind of, to some degree, business as usual."Nobody involved argues that private giving can substitute for what was cut. A study published in The Lancet in June 2025, analysing data from 133 countries, estimated that USAID-supported programmes had prevented more than 91 million deaths between 2001 and 2021, and projected that sustained cuts could result in over 14 million additional deaths by 2030, including more than 4.5 million children under five. The authors described the projection as a model output with a wide uncertainty range.Also read: Bill Gates never studied at University of Washington, but it paid him $500 as a teen; 5 decades later, Microsoft co-founder is giving it $540 millionThe Trump administration has defended the closure. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in July 2025 that the agency had little to show for itself since the end of the Cold War, and that the State Department would prioritise trade and investment over aid, negotiating directly with countries rather than through nonprofits and contractors.Squires said she hopes the anonymous gift prompts others. A donation of that size signals that people still trust both her organisation and the humanitarian sector, she told AP."It's not only up to individuals," she said. "However, individuals who have the means, who have the passion and can invest like this, will help to bring others along."(With inputs from AP)

items.title: Paras Dairy, KIS Group to set up 10 BioCNG plants with ₹1,000 cr investment

Bengaluru-based KIS Group and Paras Dairy will form a joint venture to set up 10 BioCNG plants with an investment of Rs 1,000 crore.
According to a joint statement, KIS Group and Paras Dairy have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to set up 10 BioCNG (CBG) plants across Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and other states, with an estimated investment of Rs 1,000 crore.
They will form a joint venture (JV) for the proposed BioCNG plants.
Under the partnership, KIS Group will be responsible for technology, construction and operation of the plants, while Paras Dairy will be responsible for feedstock arrangement, land and approvals.
The MoU was signed at the IBET Expo here.
Founded in 2006, KIS Group is a clean technology player specialising in Biogas, BioCNG, and BioLNG solutions. Paras Dairy has plants in Sahibabad, Guloathi and Sandila in Uttar Pradesh, Malanpur in Madhya Pradesh and Newasa in Maharashtra.

"We feel proud that 49 per cent of all real-time payments in the world are happening through India, and it's great. But I hope that other parts of the world capture a lot of the growth.

items.title: Nearly 49% Indian students eye overseas education for better jobs: Report
items.summary:
Students in India are becoming more outcome-focused, as nearly half of aspirants cite better job opportunities as their primary reason for studying abroad, a report said on Wednesday.
According to skilling and workforce development company upGrad's Transnational Education (TNE) Report 2026, around 49 per cent of Indian aspirants revealed better job opportunities as the primary reason for studying abroad, compared to other factors like quality of education, permanent residency or lifestyle aspirations.
Students in India are significantly becoming more result-oriented and are evaluating destinations based on ROI (Return on Investment), employment opportunities and long-term career outcomes over institutional prominence, the report said.
The upGrad report is based on insights from 53,800 counselled aspirants between January 2025 and June 2026.
The respondent base was mainly made up of aspirants early in their professional journeys and fresh graduates, with 65.8 per cent being freshers

items.title: Nepal flood death toll climbs to 1,365 as rescue efforts continue
items.summary:
The death toll from the devastating flash floods in Nepal climbed to 1,365 on Wednesday as more bodies were recovered from the affected areas, authorities said.
Rescue teams continued to search for 5,326 people, including at least 589 foreign nationals, who remain missing, according to a Nepal Police news bulletin.
Rescue teams recovered 363 bodies from Chitwan district, 226 from Nawalparasi East, 222 from Nawalparasi West, and 197 from Nuwakot.
Similarly, 174 bodies were recovered from Rasuwa district, 75 from Gorkha, 70 from Dhading and 38 from Tanahu.
So far, 102 bodies have been handed over to the family members after completing the identification process, police said.
Security personnel have safely kept 1,147 unidentified bodies underground in accordance with all prescribed protocols, including the collection of DNA samples to facilitate their identification.
The flash floods, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26, devastated towns and .

items.title: 'Unacceptable': India condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations
items.summary:
India on Wednesday condemned the latest wave of attacks carried out by Houthi militants on oil installations in Saudi Arabia, and said the strikes undermined regional security.
The Iran-backed Houthi militant group targeted Saudi oil facilities and some other civilian infrastructure on Tuesday, triggering widespread apprehensions about further escalation in the West Asia conflict.
India condemned the attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, especially the targeting of civilian and economic facilities, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said.
He added that such attacks that undermined regional security and stability and threatened freedom of navigation in the Bab-el-Mandeb were "unacceptable".
Jaiswal was responding to a media query.
The attacks on Saudi oil facilities came amid the US ramping up its economic sanctions against Iran.
The Houthis have been majorly operating from Yemen.

items.title: UK chaos: Flights resume but delays ahead
items.summary: Flights resumed at major UK airports on Wednesday after an air traffic control system failure cancelled more than 1,000 flights and caused delays across Britain. Heathrow and Gatwick warned that disruption could continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew.Britain’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said it had resolved the problem in its flight processing system on Tuesday evening. However, delays continued across 15 UK airports and beyond as airlines and airports worked to clear a backlog of flights.Heathrow resumed departures but suspended arrivals for the rest of Tuesday night. The airport said flights were operating today, but warned that some disruption may continue.Gatwick also said its operations would take time to return to normal.“We still anticipate that it will take time for our operations to fully return to normal,” the airport said.Passengers were left stranded on aircraft, at terminals and at baggage collection areas during the disruption.British Airways cancelled or diverted more than 100 flights. The airline said aircraft and crew had ended up in different locations, affecting its operations.“The severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact,” a British Airways spokesperson said. “This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.”Passengers on a British Airways flight scheduled to fly from Heathrow to Baltimore spent four hours on the ground before leaving the aircraft. Cabin crew served pasta and chicken curry during the delay, while some passengers watched films or walked through the aisles.Passengers later reported confusion at the baggage claim area and said they were told to file claims for their bags.At Gatwick, Josie Donoghue spent three hours on a plane before her Ryanair flight to Ireland was cancelled.“Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz,” she said, referring to the former island prison in San Francisco Bay. “It’s just an absolute nightmare down there. It’s the only word I can use to describe it.”Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers were affected and that it had cancelled more than 50 scheduled flights.EasyJet said some of its flights were “unable to operate” and that the system failure caused “delays to flights across Europe.”Other affected airports included London Stansted and London City, as well as airports in Manchester, Birmingham and Scotland. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status with their airline before travelling.

items.title: Pakistan issues warning after attack on Saudi
items.summary: Islamabad: Pakistan said there should be "no ambiguity" that an attack on any one of the three members of the newly formed Makkah Defence Alliance would be treated as an attack on all, as he warned that the pact could become operative following Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia.Defence Minister Khawaja Asif's remarks on Tuesday come hours after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting cities and economic and energy infrastructure and injuring at least 73 civilians.The minister said any unprovoked aggression against a member state, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia, would activate the collective-defence provisions of the agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah last month."There should be no ambiguity; there is no need for any clarity that this is a joint defence agreement," Asif said in an interview with Geo TV channel. Pakistan would honour its commitments to Saudi Arabia under the pact, he said."There should be no doubt about this. We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact and, God willing, we will honour them in case there is a need," Asif asserted.Asif, however, said he was not aware of any contact between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia following the Houthi attacks.He stressed that the agreement was defensive in nature and did not authorise the three countries to launch attacks against another state on their own initiative."This is not an aggressive agreement under which the three countries would, on their own initiative, attack another country. But if there is any aggression against one member state, all three member states will respond," the minister said.He expressed hope that tensions would subside, but warned the Houthis against extending the Yemen conflict beyond the country's borders."If they try to export them, the clauses of this agreement to counter aggression will become operative," Asif reiterated.Asif described the Houthis as "non-state actors" and said there was sympathy for Iran across the Muslim world, including Yemen, over its ongoing conflict with the United States.He, however, cautioned against allowing such sentiments to be used to widen an existing bilateral dispute.The minister said the Makkah alliance could serve as a deterrent and did not necessarily mean that the three countries would respond to aggression with military force."We don't need to respond to a brick with a stone," he said, arguing that the combined military capabilities of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye should themselves act as a deterrent.He said Saudi Arabia should not be dragged into what he described as an internal conflict in Yemen and expressed hope that diplomatic efforts could help prevent further escalation.A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's internationally recognised government in its war against the Houthis for more than a decade.The Houthis said Tuesday's attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi airstrikes on areas of northwestern Yemen under their control. On Monday, the group accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of Al Hazm, killing at least 11 people.

items.title: Delhi PG residents ask: Are we safe?
items.summary: New Delhi: For students and young professionals who leave their hometowns for Delhi in pursuit of their dreams, a paying guest accommodation gradually becomes much more than four walls and a bed. It becomes a second home where they return after college or work, have their meals, prepare for exams, attend late-night meetings and call their families before going to sleep.But the collapse of a five-storey building housing a boys' PG in south Delhi's Satya Niketan on September 6, which claimed seven lives, has shaken that sense of security and made many question whether the place they call home is truly safe.Also Read: Satya Niketan tragedy: Supreme Court may examine building safety, construction violations across IndiaFor students and young professionals currently living in PGs across Delhi-NCR, the tragedy has brought a question into their rooms that many had never considered before: Do I really know how safe the building I sleep in is?Until now, choosing a PG was largely about rent, food, Wi-Fi and proximity to college or the workplace. The condition of the building, its permissions and approvals, or what would happen in an emergency often remained outside that calculation.Sneha Mishra, who lives at 'New PG for Girls' in Sant Nagar, said the collapse has changed the way she looks at the place she has come to regard as home after moving to Delhi from Deoghar, Jharkhand."When I came to Delhi from Deoghar, this PG became my second home. I eat, study and sleep here, but I never really thought about whether the place I call home is actually safe," Mishra told ANI.That thought, she said, now follows her even when she is trying to sleep."Earlier, I never thought about the condition of the building. Now, when I go to sleep, there is a question in my mind - what if the building we trust with our lives is not safe?" she told ANI.The worry does not stop with the young people living inside these buildings. It travels back home, to parents who send their children to Delhi believing they have found a secure place to live."Our parents send us here believing we are safe. After Satya Niketan, many of us have started looking at the roof over our heads differently," Mishra told ANI.But for many young people, finding a safer place is not simply a matter of making a choice. It is also a matter of being able to afford one. A better-maintained PG can mean a higher monthly rent, something that can be difficult for a student or someone earning an entry-level salary. In a city where every extra thousand rupees matters, safety can end up competing with affordability.Shilpashree Mondal, who lives in a PG in Noida, stated that her budget leaves little room for choice.Also Read: Buried aspirations: Grieving families say, if this isn’t murder, what is? after losing CA and IAS aspirants to Satya Niketan PG disaster"I don't think even a working woman like me has much of a real choice when it comes to choosing where to live. Budget decides most of it, especially in a city like Delhi, where finding a safe and affordable place can be difficult," Mondal told ANI.The Satya Niketan collapse initially frightened Mondal. But soon, the fear turned into a closer look at the place where she herself lives."I started thinking, what if something like this happens to my PG too? I somehow convinced myself that it wouldn't happen, but there are already things that worry me, like problems with the water supply, poor hygiene and dampness in the walls," she said.Often, she said, the reality of a PG becomes clear only after moving in."The owner and caretakers often make things look safer and better than they actually are, but you only realise the real problems once you start living there," Mondal told ANI.For Pallavi Joshi, who hails from Uttarakhand's Haldwand has been living in a Delhi PG for nearly two years, the collapse has changed an otherwise ordinary nightly routine."I had never thought about the structure of my PG before. After Satya Niketan, I started noticing how my building is designed and wondering whether there are enough safety measures. Even at night, I sometimes think about what would happen if something went wrong here," Joshi told ANI.Joshi told ANI that neither her PG owner nor anyone from the management approached the occupants after the incident to discuss their concerns or assure them about the safety of the building.She said PG owners often focus on receiving rent on time, while concerns over safety, hygiene and what happens during an emergency receive less attention.For Vijaya Roy, a student of Delhi University's Ramanujan College preparing for the CAT examination, the uncertainty begins with something as basic as knowing whether the place has the necessary permissions.Around 20 to 25 people live in her PG, she told ANI, but occupants are not always told whether the property has the required approvals."We don't even know whether they have permission from the Municipal Corporation of Delhi or not. When we first come to the PG, they demand documents from us, but they don't show any papers to us," Roy told ANI.For Roy, students should not have to take the owner's word for it when it comes to the building they are going to sleep in every night."It should be made mandatory that tenants are able to get the papers from PG owners, so that they know whether the building has the proper permissions and whether the regulations are being followed," she said.For Delhi University students, the shortage of affordable hostel accommodation makes that dependence on PGs even greater, Roy said."If adequate hostel facilities are available in colleges, students will have another option. PG owners will not have the same monopoly and may be forced to improve conditions," she told ANI.For these students and young professionals, the Satya Niketan collapse is no longer something they simply watched on a news screen. It has changed the way they look at their own rooms at the damp patch on a wall, the makeshift partition, the crowded staircase or the roof above their bed.Keping student safety as a priority, the Delhi government is working on a comprehensive policy to regulate paying guest (PG) accommodations in the national capital, with Urban Development Minister Ashish Sood outlining a series of proposed measures aimed at strengthening safety, security and rent regulation for students.Under the proposed policy, PG operators would be required to obtain a PG Operating Licence and complete both police and municipal verification before running their establishments. The proposed rules would also make CCTV cameras mandatory at entrances and in common areas of PG accommodations, with recordings required to be preserved for 30 days.For PGs housing 15 or more students, operators would be required to employ a licensed night guard between 10 pm and 6 am. Visitor registers would also be made mandatory, while non-resident visitors would be permitted entry between 8 am and 9 pm.The policy would further require every PG to have a warden either residing at the premises or maintaining an office within a 500-metre radius. The warden would have to be physically available within 15 minutes in case of an emergency. To address concerns over arbitrary and high rents, the proposed policy envisages a Rent Regulation Committee that would determine rent bands for different areas.The rent bands would take into account factors including occupancy levels, amenities provided, prevailing market rates and the proximity of the PG to colleges and public transport. The draft framework also proposes the creation of an Institutional Accommodation Committee, comprising college officials, student representatives, a municipal representative and a police liaison officer.

Britain's National Air Traffic Services said it had resolved a problem in its flight processing system in the evening but delays rippled across 15 UK airports and beyond as airlines and airports worked to clear a huge backlog of delayed flights.
Josie Donoghue spent three hours stuck on a plane at Gatwick before her Ryanair flight to Ireland was cancelled.

items.summary:
The US military has destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers following attacks on a US warship by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, US Central Command said in a social media post on Tuesday.
The US strikes were in response to two Iranian efforts to hit the warship with ballistic missiles over the past two days, the statement added.
Iranian state television also reported the strikes, saying US forces attacked at least three Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
The latest tit-for-tat strikes come as Washington and Tehran lurch back toward fighting during more than six months of war.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will not allow Iran's attacks to go unanswered.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the latest .

Meta launched on Tuesday a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over who are looking for help with day-to-day tasks like schedules, shopping and, in the company's words, turning "long-term goals into action plans."
The parent company of Instagram and Facebook is stressing the safety and privacy features of the agent, which for now is only available in the US Muse, Meta said, runs on a dedicated, secure virtual machine that houses both the agent and the user's data.
People can message the agent in a separate app, called Muse, or message it in WhatsApp. It can handle simple tasks like sending an email or booking travel, or bigger, long-term goals like creating a yearlong exercise plan or setting up a new business.

items.summary:
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) on Tuesday began the controlled demolition of a building adjoining the structure that collapsed in south Delhi's Satya Niketan on September 6, officials said.
An MCD official said the building had been declared dangerous.
"We started demolition of the adjoining building today, and the work was stopped in the evening. The demolition exercise will resume tomorrow morning," the official said.
The building housed a girls' paying guest accommodation and was evacuated after the collapse of the neighbouring five-storey structure, which left at least seven people dead and five injured on Sunday.
The same day, the MCD issued an order for property no 13 in Satya Niketan, directing the owner or occupier to tear down the structure, citing it as a threat to residents and neighbouring buildings.
MCD officials had earlier said that the students had already vacated the building and were returning only to collect their belongings before the demolition.

The UK on Tuesday announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, banning the import of goods from the occupied Palestinian territories which it declared as "illegal".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband was joined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in the House of Commons as he delivered a statement to condemn the "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in West Bank settlements.
While highlighting his own "proud British Jew" heritage, Miliband announced a "new comprehensive sanctions regime with appropriate religious exemptions".
"The government believes the unlawfulness of the occupation should be reflected in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories," Miliband told MPs.
"So I can announce today that we will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories," he said.
Miliband said action would be taken against specific companies and individuals providing construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate

items.title: ChrysCapital eyes stake in Linux Labs
items.summary: Mumbai: Homegrown private equity firm ChrysCapital is set to acquire a 20-25% stake in central nervous system (CNS)- focused domestic formulations company Linux Laboratories for around $60-65 million (₹600 crore), people aware of the development told ET. Tata Capital Healthcare Fund, an existing investor in Chennai-based Linux Laboratories, will exit its entire 15% stake as part of the transaction, while ChrysCapital will acquire an additional 5-10% stake through a primary capital infusion.Presently, founders Keerthivasan K, Ananda Kumar Sundharam and Hariharan Parameswaran together hold 84.68%. Tata Capital Healthcare Fund II holds a 15.32%, Tracxn data showed. Tata Capital Healthcare Fund invested ₹80 crore in Linux in 2021.Also read: Pharma sector must attract more investment in clinical trials, R&D: Piyush GoyalFounded in 2007, Linux has a portfolio of more than 64 brands across around 180 products, spanning therapeutic segments such as neurology, psychiatry and cosmetic dermatology.Linux Laboratories is expected to post a revenue of ₹450-500 crore and an Ebitda of ₹85-90 crore in FY27, said sources.Mails sent to Linux Laboratories and ChrysCapital remained unanswered until the publication of this report, while a Tata Capital spokesperson declined to comment. Private equity interest in India's pharmaceutical formulations sector has remained strong, particularly in domestic branded-generics businesses with established brands and exposure to chronic and specialtiy therapies.133939521In 2024, ChrysCapital invested about $70 million in La Renon Healthcare at a valuation of around $800 million, while the firm has also backed companies such as Mankind Pharma, Eris Lifesciences, Torrent Pharmaceuticals and Ipca Laboratories.Kunal Shroff, managing partner at ChrysCapital, believes that geopolitical issues have a relatively limited impact on ChrysCapital's portfolios. In the pharma segment, most of the portfolio companies are domestically focused, and they continue to grow with strong margins and healthy returns on equity, he told ET last year. In July, ChrysCapital had acquired a controlling 70.68% stake in Novartis India (NIL), with major brands such as Voveran, Calcium Sandoz and Tegretol.Since its inception in 1999, ChrysCapital has cumulatively raised close to $8.5 billion across 10 PE funds, a continuation vehicle, and its public markets fund. Through its PE funds, it has deployed over $5.5 billion in more than 110 portfolio companies.Also read: Sun Pharma gets ratings boost from Moody's, S&P over USD 11.75-bn Organon & Co acquisition bidThe Indian pharmaceutical industry ranks 3rd globally by volume and 11th by value. The domestic pharmaceutical market, valued at $60 billion, is projected to reach $130 billion by 2030, according to the Government of India. India is the largest global supplier of generic medicines, accounting for around 20% of global supply, manufacturing 60,000 generic brands across 60 therapeutic categories.

items.summary: Patna, More than 35 lakh people in 14 districts of Bihar were affected by floods as the situation worsened on Tuesday, with authorities sounding an alert for areas downstream of the Ganga as the river crossed the highest flood level at Sultanganj in Bhagalpur district.A boat carrying 11 people capsized on the Ganga in Vaishali, leading to one death while another remained missing, officials said, adding that nine people have been rescued.Officials said the floods have affected 35.89 lakh people in 14 districts -- Patna, Bhojpur, Saran, Vaishali, Bhagalpur, Begusarai, Buxar, Samastipur, Munger, Katihar, Lakhisarai, Khagaria, Purnea and Arwal.On Monday, 29.13 lakh people in 13 districts were impacted by the deluge, caused by overflowing rivers fed by heavy rainfall.According to the meteorological department, the state recorded 79.6 mm of rainfall so far in September, which is 31 per cent above the normal.The Disaster Management Department said that in Bhagalpur's Sultanganj, the Ganga was flowing at 36.80 metres at 8 am, surpassing its previous highest flood level of 36.75 metres recorded on August 17, 2021.Several other rivers, including the Gandak, Kosi, Budhi Gandak, Ganga, Punpun, Bagmati and Ghaghra, were also flowing above their danger levels at multiple locations.The waters of the Gandak river at Dumriaghat and Hajipur, Kosi at Baltara and Kursela, Budhi Gandak at Khagaria, Ganga at Digha, Gandhi Ghat, Hathidah, Bhagalpur, Kahalgaon and Munger were above the danger level."A total of 456 community kitchens were being operated in various districts. Also, 14 relief camps are being run, where arrangements have been made for accommodation, food, medical care and other essential services," the Disaster Management Department said.A total of 1,876 boats have been pressed into service for relief and rescue operations, it said. Also, 27 teams of the State Disaster Response Force and 10 of the National Disaster Response Force have been deployed for rescue operations.The statement said the Gandak Barrage discharged 92,900 cusecs of water at 6 pm on Tuesday, while the Kosi Barrage let out 1,61,135 cusecs of water at 6 pm.RJD president Lalu Prasad on Tuesday voiced dissatisfaction with the BJP government's flood control measures in Bihar and called for a "permanent solution" to the recurring calamity.In a social media post, the former chief minister also stressed the need for a "straight talk" with Nepal, since floods in rivers originating in the neighbouring country often cause devastation in north Bihar."There must be a straight talk with Nepal on river management. This is an issue that had been raised even by late Karpoori Thakur. The problem calls for a permanent solution", said the RJD supremo, referring to his mentor who was the chief minister in the 1970s.

S&P Global Ratings assigned a preliminary 'BBB+' long-term issuer credit rating, while Moody's Ratings assigned a 'Baa1' long-term issuer rating to the Indian pharmaceutical major. Both agencies have maintained a 'stable' outlook for the company.
Baa1 and BBB+ are investment-grade credit ratings that indicate adequate payment capacity with moderate credit risk.
The rating actions follow Sun Pharma's binding bid in April 2026 to acquire a 100 per cent stake in Organon for an enterprise value of USD 11.75 billion. The transaction is expected to close by March 2027, subject to regulatory approvals.
